title: Uranium cubes reveal why the German nuclear project failed
gist: A 2026 PNAS Nexus paper by Timothy Koeth, Miriam Hiebert and co-authors finds Nazi Germany's B8 reactor at Haigerloch would have needed 1,292-1,775 uranium cubes (vs. 664 used) and twice the wartime heavy-water output of Norsk Hydro's Vemork plant to reach criticality, contradicting Werner Heisenberg's claim that it was close. Impure Ruhr graphite caused by the British blockade made any natural-uranium, graphite-moderated pile infeasible; this is a science-history piece with little direct market signal.

insights.claim: The new PNAS Nexus analysis calculates the German B8 reactor would have needed 1,292 to 1,775 uranium cubes to achieve criticality, versus the 664 cubes actually used.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Historical illustration that fuel inventory, not just design, gates reactor viability.
insights.quote: Our calculations suggest Heisenberg significantly underestimated the materials required

insights.claim: The B8 design would also have required twice the heavy water produced by Norsk Hydro's Vemork plant in Norway, the sole source at the time, over the entire war.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Single-source moderator supply was a binding strategic bottleneck, a parallel to modern nuclear supply-chain concentration.

insights.claim: Werner Heisenberg claimed the B8 pile needed only a slight size increase to work, and a 2009 model suggested 50% more cubes would suffice; the new paper rejects both as underestimates.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Overturns a long-standing historical narrative about how close Germany came to a reactor.

insights.claim: Koeth and Hiebert's earlier archival work found about 400 additional cubes from the separate Gottow group, initially suggesting the isolated German groups' failure to share resources hampered the program; the new paper reaches a different conclusion.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Shows how new physical evidence can revise earlier organizational explanations.
insights.locator: Koeth and Hiebert uncovered a box

insights.claim: Koeth attributes German delays despite a two-year head start to fierce competition over finite resources, interpersonal rivalries and ineffectual scientific management across three isolated groups in Berlin, Gottow and Leipzig.
insights.speaker: Timothy Koeth
insights.so_what: A management lesson for large state-led technology programs.
insights.quote: fierce competition over finite resources, bitter interpersonal rivalries, and ineffectual scientific management

insights.claim: The January 1940 British naval blockade cut Germany off from petroleum coke, forcing use of Ruhr metallurgical coke with twice the impurities of American coke, so no natural-uranium graphite-moderated pile could have gone critical with German materials.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Materials purity and access to feedstocks can decide strategic technology races.
insights.quote: no natural uranium, graphite-moderated pile could have gone critical
insights.locator: The authors also cited prior work
